findings.title: Use of `resp_start_line` variable in server-side code path causes NameError
findings.description: On line 253, when `self.is_client` is False (server mode), the code references `resp_start_line.code` which was only assigned in the `if self.is_client:` branch (line 200). In server mode, `resp_start_line` is never defined, so this reference will raise a `NameError` at runtime for any server-side request that has a body. The expression `resp_start_line.code if self.is_client else 0` evaluates `resp_start_line` even in the else branch because Python evaluates both sides of a ternary... actually Python does short-circuit ternary, so `resp_start_line` is only evaluated when `self.is_client` is True. Wait - actually the ternary `A if condition else B` only evaluates A when condition is True. So `resp_start_line.code` is only evaluated when `self.is_client` is True, which means `resp_start_line` is always defined in that path. This is safe. Re-examining: this is not actually a bug.
findings.suggestion: No action needed; Python ternary expressions are short-circuit evaluated.

findings.title: Missing ValueError handling for invalid chunk size in chunked body parsing
findings.description: In `_read_chunked_body`, line 663 calls `int(chunk_len_str.strip(), 16)` without wrapping it in a try/except. If a malicious or malformed client sends a non-hexadecimal chunk size line, this will raise an unhandled `ValueError` that propagates up through `_read_message`. This exception is not a `httputil.HTTPInputError`, so it will not be caught by the `except httputil.HTTPInputError` handler on line 288. Instead it will be caught by the generic `except Exception` in `_server_request_loop` (line 825) which logs an error and closes the connection, but also logs an `Uncaught exception` error unnecessarily. The connection is closed abruptly without sending a proper 400 response to the client.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the `int()` call in a try/except ValueError and raise `httputil.HTTPInputError` instead: `try: chunk_len = int(chunk_len_str.strip(), 16) except ValueError: raise httputil.HTTPInputError('invalid chunk size')`

findings.title: AssertionError instead of proper error for malformed chunked body terminator
findings.description: On line 687, the code uses `assert crlf == b'\r\n'` to validate that each chunk is properly terminated with CRLF. In production Python (running with `-O` flag, i.e. optimized mode), `assert` statements are disabled and this check is completely skipped, allowing malformed chunked bodies to be silently accepted. Even without optimization, an `AssertionError` is raised instead of a `httputil.HTTPInputError`, which means it is not caught by the appropriate error handler on line 288 and will result in the generic exception handler being invoked, logging an error without sending a 400 response.
findings.suggestion: Replace the assert with a proper check: `if crlf != b'\r\n': raise httputil.HTTPInputError('improperly terminated chunk')`

findings.title: Incomplete HTTP header injection prevention (only checks for newline, not carriage return)
findings.description:
On lines 448-449, the code checks for `b'
'` in header lines to prevent header injection, but does not check for standalone `b''` (bare carriage return). While many HTTP parsers treat `` alone as a line terminator, a crafted header value containing only `` (without `
`) could potentially be used for header injection against vulnerable downstream parsers or proxies. The check on line 448 `if b'
' in line` would not catch a header value like `ValueX-Injected: evil`.
findings.suggestion: Also check for `b'\r'` in header lines: `if b'\n' in line or b'\r' in line: raise ValueError(...)`

findings.title: Gzip decompression bomb: no limit on decompressed data size
findings.description: In `_GzipMessageDelegate.data_received` (lines 724-734), gzip-compressed data is decompressed in a loop using `self._decompressor.decompress(compressed_data, self._chunk_size)` and then continuing with `self._decompressor.unconsumed_tail`. While each decompression call is limited to `chunk_size` bytes of output, there is no overall limit on the total amount of decompressed data. A malicious client can send a small gzip payload (a 'zip bomb') that decompresses to an extremely large body, far exceeding `self._max_body_size`. The body size limit on line 621 (`content_length > self._max_body_size`) checks the compressed Content-Length, not the decompressed size, allowing an attacker to bypass the body size limit with a highly compressed payload.
findings.suggestion: Track the total decompressed bytes in `_GzipMessageDelegate` and raise an error if it exceeds `_max_body_size`. Pass the max body size into the delegate and check on each decompressed chunk.

findings.title: HTTP header parsing: eol=-1 when no newline found leads to incorrect start_line parsing
findings.description: In `_parse_headers` on line 581, `data_str.find('\n')` returns -1 if no newline is found. While in practice `read_until_regex` guarantees the data contains the header terminator, if for any reason `data_str` has no `\n` (e.g., edge cases with the lstrip removing all content), `eol` will be -1, causing `data_str[:eol]` to return all characters except the last one (Python slice behavior with -1), giving an incorrect start line. This could cause silent misparsing instead of raising an appropriate error.
findings.suggestion: Check if `eol == -1` after the find and raise an `httputil.HTTPInputError` if no newline is found in the header data.

findings.title: Mutable default argument `set()` for `exclude` parameter in `serialize_response`
findings.description: The `exclude` parameter in `serialize_response` (line 78) uses a mutable `set()` as a default argument. In Python, mutable default arguments are created once at function definition time and shared across all calls that use the default. If any caller modifies the passed-in set (or if the set object is mutated internally), this shared default object will be permanently altered, causing unexpected behavior in subsequent calls that rely on the default value.
findings.suggestion: Use `None` as the default value and replace it with a new `set()` inside the function body: `exclude: Union[SetIntStr, DictIntStrAny] = None` and then `exclude = exclude or set()`.

findings.description: The `response_model_exclude` parameter in `get_request_handler` (line 131) uses a mutable `set()` as a default argument. This is the same class of bug as described for `serialize_response`: the same set object is shared across all calls using the default, so mutations to it persist globally.
findings.suggestion: Use `None` as the default and convert it inside the function: `response_model_exclude = response_model_exclude if response_model_exclude is not None else set()`.

findings.title: Non-deterministic `unique_id` generation when `methods` is a `Set`
findings.description: On line 271, `list(methods)[0]` is used to pick the first method for `generate_operation_id_for_path`. When `methods` is a `Set[str]` (which is allowed by the type signature on line 252), iteration order is not guaranteed in Python, meaning the `unique_id` could be non-deterministic across runs or Python versions. This also affects `self.methods` on line 269 which converts to a set again after potentially receiving a set. While `self.methods` is correctly normalized to uppercase, the `unique_id` depends on an arbitrary element from the original `methods` collection before it has been normalized to a set.
findings.suggestion: Normalize `methods` to a sorted list before selecting the first element: `method=sorted(self.methods)[0]` (using the already-normalized `self.methods`).

findings.title: Empty-prefix route validation only checks `APIRoute`-like routes with a `path` attribute
findings.description: In `include_router` when `prefix` is empty, the code iterates over `router.routes` and checks `getattr(r, 'path')` to ensure no route has an empty path. However, the condition `if path is not None and not path` is effectively checking that path is not `None` and is falsy (empty string). But this relies on `getattr(r, 'path')` which will raise an `AttributeError` if the attribute doesn't exist since no default is provided in the second argument—though typically routes have a path attribute. More importantly, if `path` is `None` (i.e., `getattr` returns `None` because the route has no `path` attribute), the condition short-circuits and the route passes validation silently even if it could result in an effectively empty combined path.
findings.suggestion: Provide a default value in `getattr`: `path = getattr(r, 'path', None)` (which is already what occurs since the None check exists). Clarify the intent: check if `path is not None and not path` raises for routes with genuinely absent path attributes by using `getattr(r, 'path', None)`.

findings.title: Non-deterministic method selection for unique_id generation when methods is a Set
findings.description: At line 316, `list(methods)[0]` is used to pick the first method for generating the unique operation ID. However, `methods` can be passed as a `Set[str]` (see the type annotation on line 290), and sets in Python have no guaranteed iteration order. This means that for an endpoint registered with multiple HTTP methods, the `unique_id` (and consequently OpenAPI operation IDs, response field names, etc.) may differ between Python interpreter runs or even between invocations in the same process. While `self.methods` at line 314 is always a set, the original `methods` variable is used at line 316 before it is necessarily converted. If `methods` was already a set (passed by the caller), `list(methods)[0]` is non-deterministic. This can cause inconsistent OpenAPI schemas and make response_field names (line 323) unpredictable.
findings.suggestion: Sort the methods before picking the first element to ensure determinism: `method=sorted(methods)[0]`. Alternatively, use `list(self.methods)[0]` after the set has been created, but also sort it first: `method=sorted(self.methods)[0]`.

findings.title: Unhandled exception when request body is invalid JSON causes generic 400 instead of structured validation error
findings.description: At lines 182-184, when parsing a non-form body, `request.body()` is called first (line 182), and then `request.json()` is called (line 184) only if `body_bytes` is non-empty. The `json.JSONDecodeError` handler at line 185 provides a structured `RequestValidationError` with position information. However, `request.json()` in Starlette internally uses `json.loads` and will raise `json.JSONDecodeError`. This is caught correctly. But if `request.body()` itself raises (e.g., a disconnect or read error), it falls into the generic `Exception` handler at line 187, which raises a plain HTTP 400 without validation detail. More importantly, if `request.json()` raises a `UnicodeDecodeError` (which is not a subclass of `json.JSONDecodeError`), it would also fall to the generic handler and lose structured error information. This is a functional defect where the caller receives less information than intended.
findings.suggestion: Also catch `UnicodeDecodeError` alongside `json.JSONDecodeError` to produce a structured validation error. Consider wrapping the `UnicodeDecodeError` in a `RequestValidationError` with appropriate location info.

findings.title: Background tasks silently lost when raw Response already has a background task set
findings.description: At lines 205-208, when the endpoint returns a raw `Response` object directly, the code only assigns `background_tasks` to `raw_response.background` if `raw_response.background is None`. If the response already has a background task set by the endpoint, the dependency-injected `background_tasks` collected during dependency resolution are silently discarded. This means any background tasks registered via `BackgroundTasks` in dependencies will not be executed when the endpoint returns a `Response` directly with its own background task.
findings.suggestion: Merge the background tasks rather than discarding them. For example, if `raw_response.background` is already set, combine both by iterating the tasks and adding them together, or use a `BackgroundTasks` object that supports multiple tasks.

findings.title: Incorrect empty-path validation logic in include_router
findings.description: When `prefix` is empty, the code iterates over `router.routes` and checks `if path is not None and not path` (line 622) to detect routes with empty paths. However, `getattr(r, 'path')` (line 620) without a default value will raise `AttributeError` if a route object does not have a `path` attribute (e.g., a `Mount` or custom route type). Additionally, the guard condition `if path is not None and not path` will skip the validation check if `path` is `None`, meaning that a route with `path=None` silently bypasses the guard. The intent seems to be raising an exception whenever both prefix and path are empty, but a `None` path evades the check, while a missing `path` attribute causes an unhandled exception.

findings.title: Incorrect operator precedence in boolean condition for autoescape replace logic
findings.description:
The condition on lines 201-205 reads:
```python
if (
    hasattr(old, '__html__')
    or hasattr(new, '__html__')
    and not hasattr(s, '__html__')
):
```
Due to Python's operator precedence, `and` binds more tightly than `or`, so this is evaluated as:
```python
if hasattr(old, '__html__') or (hasattr(new, '__html__') and not hasattr(s, '__html__')):
```
The intended logic is likely:
```python
if (hasattr(old, '__html__') or hasattr(new, '__html__')) and not hasattr(s, '__html__'):
```
With the current code, if `old` has `__html__` but `s` also has `__html__`, then `s = escape(s)` is still executed, which will double-escape the already-HTML string `s`. Conversely, if `new` has `__html__` and `s` also has `__html__`, the `and not hasattr(s, '__html__')` short-circuits the second branch, so `s` falls into `soft_str(s)` instead of being escaped — incorrectly stripping the Markup wrapper. This leads to incorrect escaping behavior in autoescape mode.
findings.suggestion:
Add explicit parentheses to encode the correct intent:
```python
if (hasattr(old, '__html__') or hasattr(new, '__html__')) and not hasattr(s, '__html__'):
    s = escape(s)
else:
    s = soft_str(s)
```

findings.title: do_xmlattr only checks for space characters in keys but not other invalid XML attribute name characters

For example, characters like `>`, `<`, `/`, `=`, or quotes in attribute names (though unlikely in practice) are not rejected. While `escape(key)` is called, if a key contains a `>` or `=` character, the resulting HTML attribute string could be malformed. However, if a caller explicitly passes `default=None` intending to use `None` as a sentinel fill value for missing attributes, the guard prevents it from being applied and the `Undefined` object leaks through. This is inconsistent with the documented interface — there's no way to use `None` as an explicit default value.

```python

    ...

```

findings.title: Truthiness check on iterable skips empty collections silently
findings.description: In `sync_do_map` (and the async variant `do_map` at line 1514), the guard `if value:` evaluates the truthiness of the iterable before processing. For containers such as lists, dicts, or strings, an empty container is falsy and no items will be yielded, which is arguably expected. However, for custom iterables or generators that define `__bool__` as always `True` or lack a `__len__`, this check is unreliable and may either skip valid data or consume the iterator's state. More critically, for a non-empty value that happens to be falsy (e.g., a custom object returning `False` from `__bool__` but still being iterable), the mapping is silently skipped, returning an empty result instead of applying the filter — a silent incorrect computation. findings.suggestion: Remove the `if value:` guard or replace it with an explicit `None` check (`if value is not None:`). The individual iteration loop will naturally handle empty iterables without needing an upfront truthiness test.

findings.title: Dead code and unreachable None check in convert_value
findings.description: In `convert_value`, the `elif isinstance(value, datetime):` branch at line 325 contains an inner `if value is None: pass` check at line 326. This is logically impossible: if `isinstance(value, datetime)` is True, then `value` cannot be `None`. The `None` guard is placed after the isinstance check, making it unreachable dead code. More critically, the actual intent was likely to guard against `value is None` before calling `.date()` or `.time()` on it. If a database returns `None` (NULL) and the output_field is a `DateField` or `TimeField` (not `DateTimeField`), the code reaches line 325, fails the `isinstance(value, datetime)` check (since `None` is not a datetime), falls through to `return value`, and returns `None` — which happens to be safe. However, the logic is clearly inverted from the intended design. The guard should be `if value is None: pass` at the outer level before the isinstance checks, meaning the None check was meant to short-circuit the entire block. The current structure suggests a refactoring mistake where the None guard was moved inside the wrong branch.

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized LIKE pattern interpolation
findings.description: The functions mysql_contains (line 20), mysql_starts_with (line 24), mysql_ends_with (line 28), mysql_insensitive_contains (line 36), mysql_insensitive_starts_with (line 40), and mysql_insensitive_ends_with (line 44) directly interpolate the `value` parameter into LIKE pattern strings using f-strings (e.g., `f"%{value}%"`). The `value` string is not escaped before being embedded in the LIKE expression. If `value` contains the SQL LIKE wildcard characters `%` or `_`, those characters will be interpreted as wildcards by MySQL, altering the intended query semantics. More critically, if the underlying query builder does not properly parameterize the resulting literal string (i.e., if the constructed expression is rendered as a raw SQL string rather than a bound parameter), an attacker-controlled `value` can inject arbitrary SQL fragments. Even if only wildcard injection is possible, this allows matching far more rows than intended, potentially leaking data. For the insensitive variants, the pattern is passed to `functions.Upper()` rather than as a bound parameter, increasing the risk of SQL injection depending on how pypika renders that call.
findings.suggestion: Escape LIKE special characters (`%`, `_`, and the escape character itself) from `value` before embedding it in the LIKE pattern. For example, use a helper like: `escaped = value.replace('\\', '\\\\').replace('%', '\\%').replace('_', '\\_')` and then pass `f"%{escaped}%"` to `.like()`. Ideally, use parameterized queries with explicit ESCAPE clauses rather than string interpolation. Also verify that pypika renders the pattern argument as a bound parameter rather than inline SQL.

findings.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via unescaped file names in directory index HTML
findings.description: The `_directory_as_html` method constructs HTML output by directly interpolating file and directory names (and the path) without HTML-escaping them. If a file or directory name contains characters like `<`, `>`, `&`, or `"`, the resulting HTML will be malformed or exploitable. An attacker who can create files with specially crafted names on the server filesystem could inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript into the served directory listing page, leading to stored XSS.
findings.suggestion: Use `html.escape()` on `file_name`, `file_url`, `rel_path`, `relative_path_to_dir`, and `index_of` before inserting them into the HTML template. For example: `file_name = html.escape(_file.name)` and `file_url = html.escape(self._prefix + '/' + rel_path)`.

findings.title: HTTPNotFound raised as class instead of instance
findings.description: On line 670, `raise HTTPNotFound` raises the class object itself rather than an instance of the exception (`raise HTTPNotFound()`). In Python, raising a class that is not an instance of `BaseException` directly works only if the class is an exception class (Python will instantiate it with no args), but if `HTTPNotFound.__init__` requires arguments or has side effects on instantiation, this could cause unexpected behavior or a `TypeError`. More critically, it is inconsistent with the rest of the codebase (e.g., line 648, 664, 666 all use `raise HTTPNotFound()`) and may lead to a different exception being raised than intended in some Python versions or custom exception hierarchies.
findings.suggestion: Change `raise HTTPNotFound` to `raise HTTPNotFound()` to be consistent with the rest of the codebase and ensure predictable behavior.

findings.title: User-controlled regex in DynamicResource path can cause ReDoS
findings.description: In `DynamicResource.__init__`, route patterns using the `{var:re}` syntax allow users/developers to inject arbitrary regular expressions via `DYN_WITH_RE`. The user-supplied regex is directly compiled and used for matching (line 447). A maliciously crafted or accidentally complex regex (e.g., `{id:(a+)+}`) can lead to catastrophic backtracking and denial of service when matching against adversarial input strings. This is particularly dangerous because the regex is applied to every incoming HTTP request's URL path.
findings.suggestion: Consider validating or restricting the complexity of user-supplied regexes in `{var:re}` patterns, or using a regex timeout mechanism. At minimum, document the security implications of using custom regex patterns in routes.

findings.title: Potential path traversal in StaticResource.resolve via raw URL path extraction
findings.description: In `StaticResource.resolve`, the filename is extracted as `path[len(self._prefix) + 1:]` from the raw URL path (line 625). While `_handle` does resolve and validate the path against `_directory` (lines 643-645), the raw extraction here could be influenced by URL encoding tricks if `_unquote_path` doesn't fully normalize the path. The actual path traversal protection depends entirely on the `resolve()` call in `_handle` (line 643) followed by `relative_to` check (line 645). If `_follow_symlinks=True`, the `relative_to` guard is skipped, meaning symlinks pointing outside the static directory would be followed and served.
findings.suggestion: When `follow_symlinks=True`, consider implementing additional access controls or at minimum clearly documenting that symlinks can escape the configured directory. The current behavior when `follow_symlinks=True` intentionally allows serving symlinked content outside the directory, which should be explicitly acknowledged as a security trade-off.

findings.title: Path traversal check in url_for not enforced when follow_symlinks=True
findings.description: In `StaticResource.url_for`, when `append_version=True`, the code resolves `filepath` and then checks `filepath.relative_to(self._directory)` only if `not self._follow_symlinks` (lines 578-579). When `follow_symlinks=True`, this check is skipped entirely. An attacker who can influence the `filename` argument to `url_for` with a path like `../../etc/passwd` could potentially read and hash arbitrary files on the filesystem, leaking their SHA-256 hash via the version query parameter.
findings.suggestion: Apply the `relative_to` check regardless of `follow_symlinks`, or at minimum verify that the resolved path is still under the static directory even when following symlinks.

findings.title: MaskDomain wildcard matching may allow domain spoofing
findings.description: The `MaskDomain` class converts `*` to `.*` in a regex pattern (line 821) and uses `fullmatch` (line 829). The `re_part` validation regex (line 817) allows `*` in domain labels, but the conversion to `.*` means a wildcard matches any character including `.`. For example, a mask of `*.example.com` would match `evil.attacker.com.example.com` due to the greedy `.*` matching. This could allow unintended domains to pass the domain matching check.
findings.suggestion: Replace `*` with `[^.]*` instead of `.*` in the mask compilation (line 821) to ensure wildcards only match within a single domain label and cannot span across dots.

findings.title: Path traversal via get_path normalization allows escape from static directory on some inputs
findings.description: The `get_path` method calls `os.path.normpath(os.path.join(*scope['path'].split('/')))`. When `scope['path']` is an empty string or just '/', `split('/')` produces `['', '']` or `['', '', '']`, causing `os.path.join` to start from the current working directory. For example, an empty path yields `os.path.normpath(os.path.join('', ''))` which returns `'.'`. More critically, `os.path.normpath` on Windows resolves backslashes, but the primary issue is that after splitting on '/', the first element is always an empty string. When `os.path.join` receives a list that starts with '' it doesn't anchor to any base, so the constructed path is relative. While `lookup_path` does apply `commonprefix` checks, the path normalization in `get_path` is fragile—using `posixpath` components to manually reconstruct the path rather than stripping a known prefix from `scope['path']` is the safer approach. On Windows, a path like `/C:/Windows/System32/file` would split into `['', 'C:', 'Windows', 'System32', 'file']` and `os.path.join('', 'C:', ...)` would yield `C:\Windows\System32\file`, which is an absolute path that could escape the static directory if the `commonprefix` check is bypassed (e.g., directory is `C:\static` and full_path is `C:\Windows\...` — `commonprefix` compares character-by-character, so `C:\` matches `C:\` prefix but the check compares against `directory` which is `C:\static`, so `C:\Windows` vs `C:\static` would correctly fail the prefix check; however the behavior is platform-dependent and fragile).
findings.suggestion: Use `scope['path'].lstrip('/')` or `urllib.parse` to safely extract the relative path component. Alternatively, use `pathlib.PurePosixPath` to parse the URL path and then convert to OS path. The `commonprefix` check in `lookup_path` provides a backstop but is not reliable enough on its own for all platforms.

findings.title: Path traversal check uses os.path.commonprefix which is not directory-aware
findings.description: `os.path.commonprefix` operates on strings character-by-character, not path-component-by-component. For example, if the static directory is `/static/foo` and the resolved full_path is `/static/foobar/secret.txt`, then `os.path.commonprefix(['/static/foobar/secret.txt', '/static/foo'])` returns `/static/foo`, which equals `directory`, so the check passes even though `/static/foobar/` is outside `/static/foo/`. An attacker could potentially access files in sibling directories named with a shared prefix. The correct check should verify that `full_path` starts with `directory + os.sep` (or use `pathlib.Path.is_relative_to()` in Python 3.9+).
findings.suggestion: Replace the commonprefix check with a path-component-aware check: `full_path_obj = pathlib.Path(full_path)` and `directory_obj = pathlib.Path(directory)`, then check `full_path_obj.is_relative_to(directory_obj)` (Python 3.9+). Alternatively, ensure the directory string ends with `os.sep` before comparing: `if not (full_path + os.sep).startswith(directory + os.sep): continue`.

findings.title: get_path returns '.' for root path '/' causing incorrect behavior
findings.description: When `scope['path']` is `'/'`, `scope['path'].split('/')` returns `['', '']`. Then `os.path.join('', '')` returns `''`, and `os.path.normpath('')` returns `'.'`. This means a request to the root URL will attempt to look up the path `'.'` in each directory, which resolves to the directory itself. For HTML mode this may accidentally serve the directory listing or index.html from the root, but for non-HTML mode it would find the directory stat result, not match as a regular file, and fall through to a 404. This is a logic defect that produces unexpected path resolution for the root path.
findings.suggestion: Strip the leading '/' from `scope['path']` before normalization: `path = scope['path'].lstrip('/')`. Then split and normalize only the remaining components, or use `os.path.normpath(scope['path'].lstrip('/'))` directly.

findings.title: Race condition in config_checked flag under concurrent ASGI requests
findings.description: The `config_checked` flag is read and set without any locking or synchronization. In an async context with concurrent requests, multiple coroutines can simultaneously observe `config_checked == False` and all execute `check_config()` concurrently. While this is not a security vulnerability per se, it could lead to redundant work. More importantly, if `check_config()` raises a `RuntimeError`, it could propagate to multiple requests unexpectedly. Since `config_checked` is set to `True` only after `check_config()` completes, under high concurrency many requests may all call `check_config()` before any sets the flag.
findings.suggestion: Use an `asyncio.Lock` to guard the config check, or use an `asyncio.Event` to signal completion. Alternatively, convert the check to a startup lifespan event rather than lazy initialization.

findings.title: PermissionError mapped to HTTP 401 instead of HTTP 403
findings.description: When a `PermissionError` occurs while looking up a file path (e.g., due to OS-level permission denial), the code raises `HTTPException(status_code=401)`. HTTP 401 means 'Unauthorized' and implies that authentication may resolve the issue (it should include a `WWW-Authenticate` header). HTTP 403 'Forbidden' is the semantically correct response when the server has the file but is not permitted to serve it due to OS permissions. Using 401 here could confuse clients into thinking that providing credentials would grant access to OS-restricted files.
findings.suggestion: Change `raise HTTPException(status_code=401)` to `raise HTTPException(status_code=403)` to correctly indicate that access is forbidden, not that authentication is required.

findings.title: Unsanitized user-controlled input passed to SQL ILIKE filter
findings.description: The `name_filter` query parameter value is directly interpolated into an SQLAlchemy `ilike` call using an f-string: `orm.User.name.ilike(f'%{name_filter}%')`. While SQLAlchemy parameterizes the resulting query, special LIKE wildcard characters such as `%` and `_` in the user-supplied `name_filter` are not escaped. This allows a user to craft filter strings that match unintended patterns, potentially leaking information about usernames. For example, `name_filter=a_b` would match 'aXb', 'ayb', etc. beyond the intended exact prefix/suffix matching behavior. Depending on the database backend, this may also have performance implications (DoS via expensive wildcard queries).
findings.suggestion: Escape SQL LIKE wildcard characters (`%`, `_`) in `name_filter` before using it in the `ilike` call, e.g., use SQLAlchemy's `escape` parameter or manually replace `%` with `\%` and `_` with `\_`. Also consider adding a maximum length validation on `name_filter`.

findings.title: KeyError in sew_messages_and_reactions if reaction references unknown message

If the `reactions` list contains a `message_id` that is not in the `messages` list (e.g., due to a data inconsistency), this will throw an unhandled `KeyError`. findings.title: NameError: 'streams' variable used when stream parameter is not None
findings.description: In `bulk_access_messages`, the `streams` dictionary is only defined inside the `if stream is None:` block (lines 879-888). However, at line 899, the expression `streams.get(message.recipient_id) if stream is None else stream` is evaluated for every message in the loop. When `stream is None`, this correctly references `streams`, which was defined above. But the Python interpreter still parses `streams.get(...)` even in the `if stream is None` branch regardless—the conditional expression `A if condition else B` only evaluates one branch at runtime, so `streams` will not be accessed when `stream is not None`. However, if the `stream` parameter IS None and some other code path prevents `streams` from being assigned (e.g., an exception in the set comprehension), a `NameError` would result. More critically, if `stream` is `None` and the comprehension on line 882-888 raises, `streams` is never assigned and the loop at line 892 will fail with `NameError`. The logic is fragile and the variable scoping is error-prone.

findings.title: Off-by-one error in old_unreads_missing detection
findings.description: The condition `total_unreads == MAX_UNREAD_MESSAGES` is used to detect whether the unread message list was truncated. However, `total_unreads` counts all rows processed, while the actual truncation happens via the slice `user_msgs[:MAX_UNREAD_MESSAGES]`. The flag should be set when the returned count equals MAX_UNREAD_MESSAGES (meaning there could be more), which is what the code does. But since `total_unreads` is incremented for every row processed (after slicing), if exactly `MAX_UNREAD_MESSAGES` messages are returned, it correctly sets the flag. However, the semantic intent is to detect if MORE unread messages exist beyond what was fetched — the correct check would be `>= MAX_UNREAD_MESSAGES`, or better, checking whether the pre-sliced query returns more than MAX_UNREAD_MESSAGES. As coded, if exactly MAX_UNREAD_MESSAGES messages exist (not more), `old_unreads_missing` is incorrectly set to True, giving a false warning to users.

Alternatively, use `total_unreads >= MAX_UNREAD_MESSAGES` and document that this may have a false positive at the exact boundary.

findings.title: LocalCache.__setitem__ crashes with TypeError when limit is None
findings.description: When `LocalCache` is instantiated with the default `limit=None` (e.g., `LocalCache()`), the `__setitem__` method executes `while len(self) >= self.limit`, which compares an integer to `None`. In Python 3, this raises a `TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'NoneType'`. This means any attempt to store a value in an unlimited `LocalCache` will raise an unhandled exception, completely breaking the intended 'no limit' semantics.
findings.suggestion: Guard against a None limit before the comparison: `while self.limit is not None and len(self) >= self.limit:`. This preserves the intended behavior where `limit=None` means no eviction.

findings.title: MultiValueDict.__deepcopy__ calls __init__ which emits spurious deprecation warning
findings.description: `__deepcopy__` calls `self.__class__()` (line 84), which invokes `MultiValueDict.__init__` with no arguments. Since `__init__` unconditionally emits a `ScrapyDeprecationWarning`, every deep copy operation (including the one triggered by `copy()` on line 142) will produce an extra spurious deprecation warning. This is a functional logic defect: internal copy mechanics should not re-trigger user-facing deprecation warnings.
findings.suggestion: Use `dict.__new__(self.__class__)` followed by direct dict initialization (bypassing `__init__`) for the deep copy case, or delegate the internal construction to a private factory that skips the warning.

findings.title: CaselessDict.get normalizes the default value unnecessarily
findings.description: `CaselessDict.get` calls `self.normvalue(def_val)` on the default value before passing it to `dict.get`. This means if a caller passes a non-string default (e.g., `None`, an integer, or a list), the `normvalue` method (overridable by subclasses) may transform or reject it unexpectedly. For the base `CaselessDict`, `normvalue` is a no-op, but subclasses that enforce value types (e.g., normalizing to bytes) will inadvertently corrupt the caller-supplied default. The standard dict `get` contract is to return the default as-is.
findings.suggestion: Do not apply `normvalue` to the default parameter: `return dict.get(self, self.normkey(key), def_val)`.

findings.title: CaselessDict.__init__ skips update when seq is a falsy but non-None value
findings.description: The condition `if seq:` on line 199 skips `self.update(seq)` not only when `seq` is `None`, but also when `seq` is any other falsy value such as an empty list `[]`, an empty dict `{}`, or an empty tuple `()`. While passing an empty collection is semantically harmless (the result is the same empty dict), passing a custom Mapping-like object that evaluates to falsy (e.g., `__bool__` returns False even when it has items) would silently skip initialization. The conventional pattern is `if seq is not None`.
findings.suggestion: Change the guard to `if seq is not None:` to correctly handle all falsy-but-valid sequence arguments.

findings.description: When `UPLOAD_KEEP_FILENAME` is True, the file is saved using `self._file_base` (and optionally `self._ext`), which are derived directly from the user-supplied filename without adequate sanitization. An attacker can supply a filename like `../../etc/cron.d/evil` and, after `os.path.splitext`, `_file_base` would be `../../etc/cron.d/evil`. This is then joined with `file_dir` via `os.path.join`, potentially resulting in the file being written outside of the intended upload directory. The partial mitigation at lines 112–113 only applies to the Windows-style path check on the `filename` header option, and `os.path.splitext` does not eliminate traversal sequences.
findings.suggestion: Apply `os.path.basename()` to the filename before splitting into base and extension, and additionally strip or reject any remaining path separators or traversal sequences. Consider using a sanitize function that removes all directory separators and rejects filenames starting with dots.

findings.title: `finalize()` does not emit `field_end` for `STATE_FIELD_NAME` state
findings.description: In `QuerystringParser.finalize()`, when parsing a querystring that ends with a field name but no equals sign or separator (e.g., `"foo"` at end-of-stream), the parser ends in `STATE_FIELD_NAME`. The `finalize()` method only calls `field_end` when `state == STATE_FIELD_DATA`, but not when `state == STATE_FIELD_NAME`. This means that a field name written to the parser at end-of-stream will never have its `on_field_end` callback fired, leading to incomplete callback sequences for consumers that rely on balanced `field_start`/`field_end` events.
findings.suggestion: In `finalize()`, also check if `self.state == STATE_FIELD_NAME` and emit `self.callback('field_end')` in that case, to ensure balanced field_start/field_end callback pairs.

findings.title: `_internal_write` returns `len(data)` instead of `length` (truncated length)
findings.description: The `_internal_write` method is called with a potentially truncated `length` parameter (the max permitted bytes to process), but at line 921 it returns `len(data)` (the full data length) rather than `length`. This causes `_current_size` in the `write()` method to be incremented by the actual data length rather than the number of bytes actually processed, potentially leading to incorrect size accounting after truncation.
findings.suggestion: Change line 921 to `return length` instead of `return len(data)` so that the returned value accurately reflects the number of bytes actually processed.

findings.title: Index access on potentially empty `value` bytes object in `parse_options_header`
findings.description: At line 104, `value[0]` and `value[-1]` are accessed without first verifying that `value` is non-empty. If the regex match group 2 produces an empty bytes object, this would raise an `IndexError`. The OPTION_RE regex `VALUE_STR` requires at least one character (it uses `+` quantifiers), so in practice this may not be triggered, but the guard is implicit on regex correctness rather than explicit code validation.
findings.suggestion: Add an explicit check: `if len(value) >= 2 and value[0] == QUOTE and value[-1] == QUOTE:` to guard against empty or single-character values.

findings.title: FileClass and FieldClass constructor parameters ignored; hardcoded File and Field used instead
findings.description: In the FormParser.__init__ method, the caller-supplied FileClass and FieldClass parameters are accepted but never used. Instead, lines 1554-1555 unconditionally assign self.FileClass = File and self.FieldClass = Field (the hardcoded defaults). All subsequent instantiation of file/field objects within the nested closures uses the local FileClass and FieldClass variables (from the constructor's parameter scope), not self.FileClass/self.FieldClass. While the closures do correctly capture the parameter-level FileClass and FieldClass, the instance attributes self.FileClass and self.FieldClass are silently wrong. Any code that later reads self.FileClass or self.FieldClass will get the wrong class. More critically, this is a logic defect that violates the documented API contract, and if a subclass or external code relies on self.FileClass or self.FieldClass, it will behave incorrectly.
findings.suggestion: Change lines 1554-1555 to: self.FileClass = FileClass and self.FieldClass = FieldClass, so that the instance attributes correctly reflect the caller-supplied classes.

findings.title: on_end callback may crash with AttributeError when vars.writer is None
findings.description: The on_end() closure at line 1739 calls vars.writer.finalize() unconditionally. However, vars.writer is only set inside on_headers_finished(), which is only called when part headers are received. If the multipart body is malformed or empty and the 'end' callback fires before any part's headers are ever completed, vars.writer will still be None (its initial value as set at line 1658). Calling None.finalize() will raise AttributeError, which is not caught anywhere in the write path, causing an unhandled exception.
findings.suggestion: Guard the call with: if vars.writer is not None: vars.writer.finalize(). Also consider whether a partially-parsed multipart body should be treated as an error.

findings.title: X-File-Name header trusted without validation in create_form_parser
findings.description: At line 1831, the function create_form_parser() unconditionally reads the X-File-Name header and passes it as the file_name to FormParser, regardless of the trust_x_headers parameter. The trust_x_headers parameter is accepted by the function signature but never checked or used anywhere in the function body. An attacker who can set the X-File-Name header can supply an arbitrary file name (e.g., with path traversal sequences like '../../../etc/passwd') which may be used directly when creating file objects, potentially enabling path traversal or file overwrite attacks depending on how the File class handles the name.
findings.suggestion: Check trust_x_headers before using the X-File-Name header: file_name = headers.get('X-File-Name') if trust_x_headers else None. Additionally, validate and sanitize the file name (e.g., use os.path.basename) before passing it to FileClass.

findings.title: Content-Length header not validated; may be negative or non-integer causing crash or incorrect behavior
findings.description: In parse_form(), the Content-Length header is read at line 1872 and converted to int at line 1873 without any validation. If Content-Length is a negative number, the expression content_length - bytes_read at line 1880 will produce a negative value, which when passed to min() with 1048576 will be negative. Calling input_stream.read() with a negative argument has implementation-defined behavior (often reads all data, bypassing the intended limit), or may raise an exception. Additionally, a non-numeric Content-Length will raise ValueError from int() conversion with no error handling. Furthermore, if content_length is float('inf'), max_readable = min(float('inf') - 0, 1048576) = 1048576, which then gets passed to input_stream.read(1048576) — this is fine, but if content_length becomes very large, overflow issues or incorrect loop termination may occur.
findings.suggestion: Validate that Content-Length is a non-negative integer before use. Catch ValueError from int() conversion. Add a check: if content_length < 0: raise ValueError('Negative Content-Length'). Also consider capping Content-Length to a configured maximum.

findings.title: Shared header_name and header_value lists not cleared between parts, causing header pollution across parts
findings.description: The header_name and header_value lists (declared at lines 1651-1652) are shared across all parts of the multipart body. Inside on_header_end() (lines 1682-1685), the lists are cleared after each header using del header_name[:] and del header_value[:]. However, the headers dict itself (line 1653) is never cleared between parts. When a new part begins (on_part_begin does nothing), old headers from the previous part remain in the headers dict. If the new part omits a header that was present in the previous part (e.g., Content-Transfer-Encoding), on_headers_finished() will read stale header values from the previous part, potentially applying an incorrect transfer encoding to the new part's data.
findings.suggestion: Clear the headers dict at the start of each new part. Either do this in on_part_begin() or at the start of on_headers_finished(). Add: headers.clear() in on_part_begin().

findings.title: data_callback with remaining=True resets mark to 0 instead of current position, may cause duplicate data delivery
findings.description: In the data_callback helper (lines 1090-1105), when remaining=True, after calling self.callback(name, data, marked_index, length), the mark is reset to 0 (line 1099) rather than being deleted. This means that in the next call to _internal_write(), the callback will be invoked again starting from position 0 of the new buffer, even if there is no actual data remaining for that field. This can cause empty or spurious callbacks, and in edge cases may deliver the beginning of the next chunk's data as if it were a continuation of the previous header field or value, leading to data corruption.
findings.suggestion: Review the intent of resetting the mark to 0. If the purpose is to accumulate data across chunks, ensure that the semantics are correct. Consider whether it would be more appropriate to keep the mark at 0 only if there is genuinely continuing data, and delete it otherwise.

findings.title: Infinite loop possible in parse_form when input_stream.read always returns data
findings.description: In parse_form() (lines 1878-1890), when content_length is float('inf'), the loop break condition at line 1889 checks len(buff) != max_readable (which is always 1048576 if the stream keeps returning full chunks) or bytes_read == content_length (which is float('inf'), never equal to a finite integer). If the underlying stream always returns exactly 1048576 bytes (e.g., an infinite stream or a slow-reading adversarial stream), the loop will never terminate, resulting in a denial of service.
findings.suggestion: Impose an explicit maximum read limit even when no Content-Length is given, using the MAX_BODY_SIZE configuration. Alternatively, rely on the parser's own max_size enforcement and break when the parser signals completion.

findings.title: StringAgg delimiter injected unsanitized into SQL template via string interpolation
findings.description: The `StringAgg` class uses a template string `"%(function)s(%(distinct)s%(expressions)s, '%(delimiter)s'%(ordering)s)"` where the `delimiter` parameter is interpolated directly into raw SQL. In `__init__`, `delimiter` is passed as a keyword argument to `super().__init__()`, which stores it in `self.extra`. When the template is rendered, `%(delimiter)s` is substituted with the raw value of `delimiter` without any escaping or parameterization. If a caller passes a delimiter containing single quotes or SQL metacharacters (e.g., `"', pg_sleep(10)--"`), this can break out of the string literal in the generated SQL, leading to SQL injection. For example, `StringAgg('field', "', malicious_sql--")` would produce malformed or malicious SQL.
findings.suggestion: Do not embed the delimiter directly in the SQL template string. Instead, use a parameterized query approach: pass the delimiter as a bound parameter (using `Value()` expression) rather than interpolating it as a literal in the template. For example, change `__init__` to wrap delimiter with `Value(delimiter)` and adjust the template to use a proper expression placeholder, ensuring the database driver handles quoting and escaping.

findings.title: check_password_hash passes unsanitized method string to _hash_internal
findings.description: The `check_password_hash` function splits the stored hash on '$' and extracts the `method` field, then passes it directly to `_hash_internal` without any validation. An attacker who can control the stored hash value (e.g., in a database compromise or a system that stores attacker-supplied hash strings) could pass a crafted method string with many colon-separated parameters or extremely large integer arguments (e.g., for scrypt's n, r, p or pbkdf2's iterations), potentially causing a denial of service via excessive memory allocation or CPU exhaustion. For example, a crafted scrypt method with enormous n/r/p values would cause `maxmem = 132 * n * r * p` to be an astronomically large allocation. Likewise, pbkdf2 with a very large iterations value would consume excessive CPU.
findings.suggestion: Validate the parsed method parameters (e.g., cap the scrypt n/r/p values and pbkdf2 iterations to reasonable maximums) before using them in the KDF computation. Also consider rejecting hash strings where the method is not one of the known/supported methods.

findings.title: safe_join does not block path components starting with '../' after normpath on Windows alt-sep paths
findings.description: The `safe_join` function normalizes the filename using `posixpath.normpath` and then checks for `..` or `../` prefixes, as well as OS alternative separators. However, on Windows, `posixpath.normpath` may not normalize backslash-based paths correctly since it is POSIX-specific. More critically, the empty-string check `if filename != ""` means empty-string filenames bypass normpath normalization. An empty string passes all the security checks (not abs, not `..`, not starting with `../`, no alt-seps) and gets appended to parts. While `posixpath.join` with an empty component is likely benign, the combination of not normalizing empty strings could lead to subtle path construction issues. Additionally, the check `filename.startswith("../")` only applies after normpath, which converts `..` to `..` — but intermediate `..` components like `a/../../../etc/passwd` become `../../etc/passwd` after normpath, which does start with `../` and would be caught. However, a filename of exactly `..` after normpath would be caught by `filename == ".."`. This appears largely correct but the empty-string bypass is a subtle edge case.
findings.suggestion: Apply `posixpath.normpath` to all filenames including empty strings (or treat empty strings as invalid). After normpath, also check if the normalized path starts with `..` (not just `../`) which is already done, but verify the empty string case is intentionally safe.

findings.title: Socket left open on connection failure in address-family loop
findings.description: Inside the loop over `addrinfos`, a new socket is created with `socket.socket(af, socket.SOCK_STREAM)` and then a connection attempt is made. If `sock.connect()` raises a `socket.error`, the code records the `reason` and continues to the next iteration of the loop — but it never closes the failed socket. Each failed connection attempt leaks a file descriptor. If all addresses fail and the `else` branch raises `SSHException`, all those sockets are leaked. Even if one succeeds, the previously-created-but-failed sockets from earlier iterations are leaked.
findings.suggestion: Close the socket in the except block before continuing to the next iteration: `except socket.error as e: reason = str(e); sock.close(); continue`.

findings.title: No validation of port number parsed from host string
findings.description: When a host string such as `'hostname:port'` is passed as `sock`, the port component is directly passed to `int()` (line 291) without any range validation. An attacker or misconfigured caller could supply a negative port, zero, or a port exceeding 65535 (e.g., `'host:99999'`). While `socket.getaddrinfo` may reject some invalid values, there is no explicit check enforcing the valid port range [0, 65535], which could lead to confusing errors or unexpected behavior depending on the OS.
findings.suggestion: After parsing the port with `int(hl[1])`, validate that it is in the range 0–65535 and raise a meaningful ValueError or SSHException if not.

findings.title: Weak key exchange algorithm (diffie-hellman-group1-sha1) listed as highest preference
findings.description: The `_preferred_kex` tuple lists `'diffie-hellman-group1-sha1'` as the first (highest preference) key exchange algorithm. This algorithm uses a 1024-bit Oakley Group 1 prime, which has been considered cryptographically weak since at least 2015 and is associated with the Logjam attack. By advertising it with highest preference, the transport will negotiate this weak algorithm whenever the server also supports it, downgrading security even when stronger options are available.
findings.suggestion: Reorder `_preferred_kex` so that stronger algorithms (e.g., `diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256`, `diffie-hellman-group14-sha1`) have higher preference. Ideally, remove `diffie-hellman-group1-sha1` entirely or place it last as a fallback only.

findings.title: Race condition on `completion_event` in `global_request`
findings.description: In `global_request`, `self.completion_event` is assigned a new `threading.Event()` at line 1004 without holding any lock. If multiple threads call `global_request` concurrently (or if `renegotiate_keys` runs concurrently), one thread's assignment to `self.completion_event` can overwrite another thread's event object before the first thread starts waiting on it. The second thread will then wait on the correct new event, but the first thread's event is now orphaned and may never be set, causing it to wait indefinitely or until the transport goes inactive.
findings.suggestion: Protect the assignment of and waiting on `self.completion_event` with a dedicated lock, or use a local event object per request rather than a shared instance attribute.

findings.title: Timeout check in `open_channel` uses wall-clock comparison susceptible to clock skew
findings.description: The timeout check at line 839 (`elif start_ts + timeout < time.time()`) uses `time.time()`, which is a wall-clock time that can go backwards or jump forward due to NTP adjustments or daylight saving time changes. If the system clock moves backward, the timeout may never trigger; if it jumps forward, it may trigger prematurely. This could cause channels to fail to open even though the timeout has not logically expired, or alternatively, cause indefinite hangs.
findings.suggestion: Use `time.monotonic()` (Python 3) instead of `time.time()` for measuring elapsed durations to avoid wall-clock issues.

findings.title: Potential infinite loop in _next_channel if channel table is full

If the channel table contains 16777215 or more active channels (or if all possible channel IDs are in use), the while loop will spin forever because `self._channels.get(chanid)` will never return None. While this is an extreme edge case in practice, a malicious peer that forces the server to open many channels could trigger this condition, causing a denial-of-service via an infinite loop in the calling thread.
findings.suggestion: Add a counter or a set-difference approach to detect when all channel IDs are exhausted and raise an SSHException rather than looping forever.

More importantly, the handler returns `[password]` for any single-field prompt, without validating whether the prompt is actually a password prompt. This could cause the password to be sent in response to an unrelated prompt (e.g., an OTP or TOTP field) if the server sends a single-field keyboard-interactive challenge that is not a password request.

The `input()` function echoes characters to the terminal, meaning passwords or other sensitive credentials are displayed in plaintext on the screen. The SSH protocol marks prompts with a `show_input` boolean specifically to indicate when input should be hidden (e.g., passwords). The code ignores this flag entirely when `show_input` is False.

findings.title: Missing error handling for invalid user IDs in do_send_direct_message_edit_typing_notification
findings.description: In `do_send_direct_message_edit_typing_notification` (lines 184-186), `get_user_by_id_in_realm_including_cross_realm` is called for each user_id without any try/except block. If an invalid or non-existent user_id is passed in `user_ids`, this will raise `UserProfile.DoesNotExist`, causing an unhandled exception. In contrast, `check_send_typing_notification` (line 76-82) properly catches this exception and raises a `JsonableError`. The inconsistency means callers of this function may receive unexpected server errors instead of a controlled error response.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the call to `get_user_by_id_in_realm_including_cross_realm` in a try/except block catching `UserProfile.DoesNotExist` and raise a `JsonableError` with an appropriate message, consistent with how `check_send_typing_notification` handles this case.

findings.title: recipient field in direct message edit typing notification uses filtered user_ids_to_notify instead of full recipient list
findings.description: On line 195, `RecipientFieldForTypingEditDirectMessage` is constructed using `user_ids_to_notify`, which is the filtered list of active users who receive typing notifications. This means deactivated users or users who have disabled typing notifications are excluded from the `recipient` field used to identify the conversation. This differs from the pattern in `do_send_typing_notification` (lines 32-34, 50-54), where the recipient list includes all participants (to identify the conversation), while `user_ids_to_notify` is separately filtered for delivery. As a consequence, the `recipient` field in the event will not consistently identify the direct message group, potentially causing clients to fail to match the notification to the correct conversation when some participants are inactive or have notifications disabled.
findings.suggestion: Build the recipient field from the full list of user IDs (or all resolved user profiles), and separately compute `user_ids_to_notify` as the filtered subset for delivery. This is consistent with the pattern used in `do_send_typing_notification`.
